verses.translation: And one{H259} of the seven{H7651} messengers{H4397} who had the seven{H7651} bowls{H7086} came{H935} and spoke{H1696} to me and said{H559}: Come{H935} and I will show{H7200} you the judgment{H4941} of the great{H1419} harlot{H2181} who sits{H3427} upon many{H7227} waters{H4325}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, H4941 — 'judgment') — the standard OT legal/judicial term (Ex 21:1, Deut 1:17, Isa 1:17, Mic 6:8). Greek uses κρίμα (krima — 'verdict/judgment'). While these can map, mishpat carries the full weight of the Torah's covenantal justice system. A back-translator could arrive at mishpat, but the word's Torah resonance is organic here.

Uses קְעָרוֹת (qe'arot, H7086 — 'bowls') — the same word used for the Tabernacle service bowls in Numbers 7:13,19,25 etc. Greek φιάλας ('vials/bowls') is generic. The Hebrew author reaches for the Tabernacle vessel vocabulary.
translation_notes: 'Harlot' for zonah (H2181) — the OT term used for Rahab (Josh 2:1), the harlot metaphor for Israel (Hos 1-3, Ezek 16, 23), and the 'strange woman' of Proverbs.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 51:13 — 'O you who dwell by many waters (מים רבים), rich in treasures, your end has come.' The harlot on many waters echoes Jeremiah's prophecy against Babylon.

verses.translation: And with her the kings{H4428} of the earth{H776} committed fornication{H2181}, and those she intoxicated{H7937} from her wine{H3196}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַמְּשַׁכֶּרֶת (hameshakkeret — 'she who intoxicates', feminine hiphil participle from shakar H7937). Greek ἐμεθύσθησαν ('were made drunk') is a passive verb. The Hebrew casts the harlot as the ACTIVE agent of intoxication — she is 'the intoxicator.' A back-translator from Greek's passive form would write נשתכרו ('they became drunk'), not give the woman an active agentive participle.

Hebrew says simply 'from her wine' (מיינה). Greek expands: 'from the wine of her fornication' (ἐκ τοῦ οἴνου τῆς πορνείας αὐτῆς). The Hebrew is more concise. Also Greek adds 'those dwelling on the earth' (οἱ κατοικοῦντες τὴν γῆν) as the subject — absent from the Hebrew, which has only the vague 'those' (אילו).
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'of her fornication' to 'wine' — absent from Hebrew.
Greek identifies 'those dwelling on the earth' as the drunk ones. Hebrew has only 'those' (אילו).
textual_notes: Jeremiah 51:7 — 'Babylon was a golden cup in YHWH's hand, making all the earth drunk (משכרת); the nations drank of her wine (מיינה), therefore the nations went mad.' The Hebrew Revelation uses the exact Jeremiah vocabulary: meshakkeret + miyyenah.

verses.translation: And he brought{H935} me into the wilderness{H4057}, and I saw{H7200} the woman{H802} sitting{H3427} upon the beast{H2416} whose appearance{H4758} was like the appearance{H4758} of roses, and it was full{H4392} of names{H8034} of reproaches, and it had seven{H7651} heads{H7218} and ten{H6235} horns{H7161}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses כְּמַרְאֵה שׁוֹשַׁנִּים (kemareh shoshannim — 'like the appearance of roses/lilies', H7799). Greek has κόκκινον (kokkinon — 'scarlet'). The Hebrew describes the color through a BOTANICAL SIMILE — the rose-red hue of the shoshannah flower. A back-translator from Greek's 'scarlet' would write שָׁנִי (shani — 'scarlet,' the standard color word) or אָדוֹם (adom — 'red'), NEVER a simile to flowers. The שׁוֹשַׁנָּה appears in Song of Songs 2:1-2 as a symbol of beauty; the beast mimics beauty. This is among the strongest one-way markers in the chapter.

Uses מִדְבָּר (midbar, H4057 — 'wilderness') — the loaded OT word for the place of Israel's testing, revelation, and encounter with God (Ex 3:1, 19:1-2, Num 14, Hos 2:14). Greek ἔρημον ('desert') is generic. The woman is found in the midbar — the place where Israel went astray after the golden calf.

Uses חֵירוּפִים (chirufim — 'reproaches/taunts', from charaf H2778). Greek βλασφημίας ('blasphemy') is a Greek religious concept. The Hebrew chirufim is the word for the taunting of enemies against YHWH (2 Ki 19:3, Isa 37:3, Neh 5:9). A back-translator would use גידופים (giddufim) for Greek blasphemy, not the OT taunt-word chirufim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'he brought me' (הביא אותי). Greek adds 'in the spirit' (ἐν πνεύματι) — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'like the appearance of roses' (botanical simile). Greek: 'scarlet' (κόκκινον, direct color). Entirely different mode of description.
translation_notes: 'Roses' for shoshannim — the Hebrew flower (possibly lily or lotus) known for its red color. The simile portrays the beast as beautiful but deceptive.
'Reproaches' for chirufim rather than 'blasphemies' — the Hebrew word means 'taunts/insults hurled at God,' not the Greek religious concept of blasphemy.
textual_notes: Song of Songs 2:1 — 'I am the rose of Sharon, the lily (shoshannah) of the valleys.' The beast is clothed in the beauty of the shoshannah — a parody of the bride.

verses.translation: And the woman{H802} was clothed{H3847} in garments{H4403} of red like the appearance{H4758} of roses, and upon her was much{H7227} gold{H2091} and goodly{H2896} stones{H68} and pearls, and a cup{H3563} of gold{H2091} in her hand{H3027} full{H4392} of impurities{H2932}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses טֻמְאוֹת (tum'ot — 'impurities', H2932) — the Levitical ritual impurity concept (Lev 5:3, 7:20-21, 15:3, 22:3, Num 19:13). Greek has βδελυγμάτων ('abominations'). These are FUNDAMENTALLY different concepts: Hebrew tum'ah is ritual/ceremonial defilement requiring purification; Greek bdelygma is moral abomination. A back-translator from Greek would use תועבות (to'evot — 'abominations'), not the Levitical tum'ah. The cup holds priestly impurity, not merely moral corruption.

Uses אֲבָנִים טוֹבוֹת (avanim tovot — 'goodly stones') — the standard OT term for precious gems (Gen 2:12, 1 Ki 10:2, 10:10, 2 Chr 9:10). Greek: λίθῳ τιμίῳ ('precious stone'). The Hebrew preserves the OT gemstone idiom.
Again uses כְּמַרְאֵה שׁוֹשַׁנִּים ('like the appearance of roses') for the color, reinforcing this is a deliberate Hebrew idiom, not a one-off.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'red like the appearance of roses' (one color with simile). Greek: πορφυροῦν καὶ κόκκινον ('purple AND scarlet' — two colors). Different.
Hebrew: 'full of impurities' (concise). Greek: 'full of abominations, and the impurity of her fornication' (γέμον βδελυγμάτων, καὶ ἀκαθάρτητα τῆς πορνείας αὐτῆς) — expanded.
translation_notes: 'Impurities' for tum'ot preserves the Levitical ritual concept — this is priestly defilement language, not generic moral language.
כּוֹס (kos, H3563 — 'cup') — the same word used for the cup of YHWH's wrath (Ps 75:8, Isa 51:17,22, Jer 25:15). The harlot's golden cup parodies YHWH's cup of judgment.
textual_notes: Jeremiah 51:7 — 'Babylon was a golden cup (כוס זהב) in YHWH's hand, making all the earth drunk.' The exact phrase 'cup of gold' (כוס של זהב) appears here, echoing Jeremiah.

verses.translation: And upon her forehead{H4696} was written{H3789} the name{H8034} of the secret{H5475}: of the great{H1419} city{H5892} Bavel{H894}, the mother{H517} of harlots{H2181} and of the impurities{H2932} of the earth{H776}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses סוֹד (sod, H5475 — 'secret/counsel/intimate council'). This is the specific OT word for the divine council (Jer 23:18 — 'who has stood in the sod of YHWH?', Amos 3:7 — 'YHWH does nothing without revealing his sod to his servants the prophets', Ps 25:14 — 'the sod of YHWH is for those who fear him'). Greek μυστήριον ('mystery') is a Greek religious/philosophical term. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as מוסטריון or use the later Hebrew רז (raz — 'mystery,' from Aramaic, Dan 2:18). The author uses the deeply Hebrew sod, rooting this in the prophetic council tradition.

Uses מִצְחָהּ (mitschah — 'her forehead', H4696) — the EXACT word for the High Priest's forehead where the golden plate engraved 'Holy to YHWH' (קדש ליהוה) was placed (Ex 28:38). The harlot bears an inscription on her forehead — an ANTI-PRIESTLY parody. Where the priest bore holiness, she bears the secret of Babylon. No back-translator would create this inversion.

Hebrew says הָעִיר הַגְּדוֹלָה בָּבֶל ('the great CITY Bavel'). Greek says Βαβυλὼν ἡ Μεγάλη ('Babylon the Great') without 'city.' The Hebrew adds 'the city' (העיר), explicitly identifying Babylon as an urban entity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'impurities of the earth' (טומאות). Greek: 'abominations of the earth' (βδελυγμάτων). Again, Levitical vs. moral vocabulary.
Hebrew: 'the great city Bavel.' Greek: 'Babylon the Great.' Hebrew adds 'city.'
translation_notes: 'Secret' for sod rather than 'mystery' — preserving the Hebrew prophetic-council concept rather than importing the Greek μυστήριον.
'Bavel' (not 'Babylon') — the Hebrew name בָּבֶל, which in Genesis 11:9 is connected to בָּלַל (balal — 'to confuse'), a Hebrew wordplay impossible in Greek.
textual_notes: The forehead inscription parodies Exodus 28:36-38 — 'You shall make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it... HOLY TO YHWH. It shall be on Aaron's forehead (מצח).' The harlot wears Babylon's name where the priest wore YHWH's holiness.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} that the woman{H802} was drinking{H8354} from the blood{H1818} of the holy ones{H6918} and from the blood{H1818} of the testimony{H5715} of Yeshua, and great{H1419} wonder was in me when I saw{H7200} her.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שֹׁתָה (shotah — 'drinking', active participle from shatah H8354). Greek μεθύουσαν ('being drunk') is a STATE of drunkenness. Hebrew describes the ACT of drinking — she is caught in the act, actively consuming blood. A back-translator from Greek 'drunk' would use שיכורה (shikorah — 'drunk'), not the active participle 'drinking.'

Uses עֵדוּת (edut, H5715 — 'testimony/covenant witness') — the specific OT word for the covenant tablets (Ex 25:16 — 'put the edut in the ark', Ex 31:18 — 'the two tablets of edut'). Greek μαρτύρων ('martyrs/witnesses') shifts to the concept of human witnesses. The Hebrew frames the blood as being from the COVENANT TESTIMONY of Yeshua, not merely from individual witnesses. A back-translator from Greek's 'martyrs' would use עדים (edim — 'witnesses'), not the covenant term edut.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'drinking' (active). Greek: 'drunk' (state). Different imagery.
Hebrew: 'testimony' (edut — covenant concept). Greek: 'martyrs' (μαρτύρων — witnesses). Different concepts.
translation_notes: תְּמִיָּה (temiyyah — 'wonder/astonishment') is a later Hebrew form without a standard Strong's number.

verses.translation: And the messenger{H4397} said{H559} to me: Why do you have wonder? I want to tell{H559} you the secret{H5475} of the woman{H802} and of the beast{H2416} upon which she sits{H3427}, and why it has seven{H7651} heads{H7218} and ten{H6235} horns{H7161}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אֲנִי רוֹצֶה לֵאמֹר (ani rotseh leimor — 'I want to tell') — a VOLITIONAL expression. Greek ἐγώ σοι ἐρῶ ('I will tell you') is a simple future declaration. The Hebrew angel DESIRES to reveal; the Greek angel simply states what he will do. This personal, volitional tone is natural in Hebrew narrative.

Hebrew: שֶׁיֹּשְׁבָה עָלֶיהָ ('upon which she SITS'). Greek: τοῦ βαστάζοντος αὐτήν ('which CARRIES her'). Different verbs — Hebrew 'sit' (yashav) vs. Greek 'carry/bear' (βαστάζω). A back-translator from Greek would use נושא (noseh — 'carries'), not 'sits.' The Hebrew portrays the woman as enthroned; the Greek portrays the beast as bearing her.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'she sits upon it.' Greek: 'it carries her.' Different relationship between woman and beast.
Hebrew: 'I want to tell you.' Greek: 'I will tell you.' Volitional vs. declarative.

verses.translation: The beast{H2416} which you saw{H7200} was{H1961}, and is not, and shall come{H935} again from the deep{H8415}, and shall go{H3212} to Sheol{H7585}; and the men{H582} of the ground{H127} shall be astonished at it when they see{H7200} the beast{H2416} that was and is not, even though it exists.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הָיָה וְלֹא הֹוֶה (hayah velo hoveh — 'was and is not'). The word הֹוֶה (hoveh — 'existing/present') shares the root הוה with the divine name YHWH (יהוה). The beast's essence is defined by LACKING the root of God's name — it 'was' (hayah) but 'is not hoveh' — it lacks divine Being. This is a profound theological wordplay that exists ONLY in Hebrew. No Greek translator would construct this, and no back-translator could recover it from Greek οὐκ ἔστι ('is not').

CRITICAL: Uses תְּהוֹם (tehom, H8415 — 'the deep') — the primordial deep from Genesis 1:2 (תְהוֹם — 'and darkness was upon the face of the deep'). Greek ἀβύσσου ('abyss') is related but tehom carries the specific Genesis creation weight. The beast rises from the pre-creation chaos.

CRITICAL: Uses שְׁאוֹל (Sheol, H7585 — the Hebrew underworld/realm of the dead). Greek has ἀπώλειαν ('destruction/perdition'). These are ENTIRELY different destinations: Sheol is a place of the dead (Gen 37:35, Num 16:30, Ps 16:10); ἀπώλεια is annihilation/ruin. A back-translator from Greek would write אֲבַדּוֹן (Avadon — 'destruction') or כִּלָּיוֹן (killayon — 'annihilation'), NOT Sheol.

Uses אַנְשֵׁי הָאֲדָמָה (anshei ha-adamah — 'men of the ground', H127). Greek: οἱ κατοικοῦντες ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ('those dwelling upon the earth'). The Hebrew defines people by their ORIGIN — formed from adamah (Gen 2:7). Greek defines them by their LOCATION — dwelling on the earth. A back-translator from Greek would write יושבי הארץ ('dwellers of the earth'), not the Genesis-laden 'men of the ground.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall go to Sheol' (realm of dead). Greek: 'goes to destruction' (ἀπώλειαν). Different destination entirely.
Hebrew: 'men of the ground.' Greek: 'dwellers of the earth.'

Greek adds an entire clause absent from Hebrew: 'whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world' (ὧν οὐ γέγραπται τὰ ὀνόματα ἐπὶ τὸ βιβλίον τῆς ζωῆς ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου).
translation_notes: 'The deep' for tehom preserves the Genesis 1:2 connection — the beast emerges from primordial chaos.
'Men of the ground' for anshei ha-adamah — humanity defined by its earthly substance, not merely its location.
textual_notes: Genesis 1:2 — 'and darkness was upon the face of the deep (tehom).' The beast's origin is the primordial chaos that preceded creation.

The hoveh/YHWH wordplay: Exodus 3:14 reveals the divine name through the root היה/הוה — 'I am that which I am' (אהיה אשר אהיה). The beast's defining characteristic is that it is NOT hoveh — it lacks divine existence.

verses.translation: And here{H3541} is a matter{H1697} that needs intelligence{H7922} and wisdom{H2451} and understanding{H8394}: the seven{H7651} heads{H7218} are seven{H7651} mountains{H2022} upon which the woman{H802} sits{H3427}. [10] And these are seven{H7651} [kings{H4428}].

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses a THREE-PART wisdom formula: שֵׂכֶל וְחָכְמָה וּתְבוּנָה (sekhel vechokhma utvunah — 'intelligence and wisdom and understanding'). This echoes the OT wisdom triad: Exodus 31:3 (Bezalel filled with חכמה ותבונה ודעת), Proverbs 2:6 ('YHWH gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding'), Daniel 1:17. Greek has ONLY ὁ νοῦς ὁ ἔχων σοφίαν ('the mind having wisdom') — ONE term. A back-translator from Greek would write שכל חכמה or דעת חכמה, not independently reconstruct the full three-part OT formula.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: three wisdom terms (intelligence, wisdom, understanding). Greek: one term (wisdom). The Hebrew preserves the OT triad; the Greek collapses it.
translation_notes: Verses 9 and 10 are partially combined in the Hebrew manuscript, with [10] as a marker in the text. מְלָכִים appears in brackets, suggesting editorial restoration.
textual_notes: The wisdom triad sekhel/chokhmah/tevunah parallels Daniel 1:17,20 and 5:11-14 where Daniel's wisdom is described with multiple terms. The audience needs Daniel-like wisdom to decode the vision.

verses.translation: And of them five{H2568} have fallen{H5307}, and one{H259} exists, and the second{H8145} does not yet exist; and when he comes{H935} he must be for a short time{H4592}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the second' (השני — ordinal). Greek: 'the other' (ὁ ἄλλος — indefinite). Different identifiers.
Hebrew: 'a short time' (זמן מועט). Greek: 'a little while' (ὀλίγον... μεῖναι — 'he must remain a little'). Greek adds 'remain' (μεῖναι) which is absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: עֲדַיִין (adayin — 'still/yet') is a later Hebrew form, common in Mishnaic Hebrew.

verses.translation: And the beast{H2416} that was{H1961} and is not, this is the eighth{H8066}, and it is of the seven{H7651}, and goes{H1980} to Sheol{H7585}.

one_way_hebrew: Again שְׁאוֹל (Sheol, H7585) vs. Greek ἀπώλειαν ('destruction/perdition'). Consistent with v8 — the Hebrew author consistently uses the Hebrew underworld concept where Greek uses annihilation language.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'goes to Sheol.' Greek: 'goes to destruction' (εἰς ἀπώλειαν ὑπάγει). Same divergence as v8.

verses.translation: And the ten{H6235} horns{H7161} which you saw{H7200} are ten{H6235} [kings{H4428}] who have not yet received{H6901} the kingship{H4438}, but they shall rule{H4910} as kings{H4428} with the beast{H2416} for a short time{H4592}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תִּמְשְׁלוּ (timshleu — 'they shall rule', from mashal H4910 — 'to rule/have dominion'). Greek: ἐξουσίαν... λαμβάνουσι ('receive authority'). The Hebrew says they RULE; the Greek says they RECEIVE AUTHORITY. Different concepts — active governance vs. delegated power. A back-translator from Greek would use יקבלו שלטון ('they will receive authority'), not the active ruling verb mashal.
Hebrew: זְמָן מוּעָט ('a short time'). Greek: μίαν ὥραν ('one hour'). The Hebrew is indefinite; the Greek specifies exactly 'one hour.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'they shall rule as kings' (active verb mashal). Greek: 'they receive authority as kings' (passive reception). Different political concept.
Hebrew: 'a short time.' Greek: 'one hour.' Different specificity.
translation_notes: מְלָכִים (melakhim — 'kings') appears in brackets in the source, suggesting editorial restoration.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:24 — 'the ten horns are ten kings who shall arise.' The imagery directly parallels Daniel's fourth beast vision.

verses.translation: And they have one{H259} thought{H4284}, and they shall give{H5414} their strength{H3581} and their might{H1369} to the beast{H2416}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַחֲשָׁבָה (machashavah, H4284 — 'thought/plan/design'). This is the OT word for deliberate intention — used for God's plans (Jer 29:11 — 'thoughts of peace, not of evil'), for evil devices (Gen 6:5 — 'every thought of his heart was only evil'), and for craftsman's design (Ex 31:4). Greek γνώμην ('opinion/purpose') is weaker. The Hebrew carries the weight of deliberate, calculated conspiracy.

Uses כּוֹחָם וּגְבוּרָתָם (kocham ugvuratam — 'their strength and their might') — TWO distinct Hebrew power words. כּוֹחַ (koach, H3581) is raw physical power/ability; גְּבוּרָה (gevurah, H1369) is warrior valor/heroic might (used for Samson's strength, David's warriors, YHWH's mighty acts). Greek: δύναμιν καὶ ἐξουσίαν ('power and authority') — a different pair entirely: Greek power + institutional authority vs. Hebrew strength + warrior valor.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'strength and might' (physical power pair). Greek: 'power and authority' (institutional power pair). Different concepts of power.

verses.translation: And they shall make{H6213} war{H4421} with the lamb{H7716}, and the lamb{H7716} shall overcome{H5329} them, for he is lord{H113} of lords{H113} and king{H4428} of kings{H4428}; and with him are the chosen ones{H972} and the believers{H539}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שֶׂה (seh, H7716 — 'lamb') — the specific Passover lamb word from Exodus 12:3-5. Consistent with ch. 21:9. The Passover connection is maintained throughout.

Uses בְּחִירִים (b'chirim — 'chosen ones', from bachar H972/H977 — 'to choose/elect'). Greek has THREE terms: κλητοὶ καὶ ἐκλεκτοὶ καὶ πιστοί ('called and chosen and faithful'). Hebrew has TWO: 'chosen ones and believers.' Greek adds 'called' (κλητοί) which is absent from Hebrew.

Hebrew order: 'lord of lords AND king of kings.' This is the order found in Deuteronomy 10:17 — 'YHWH your God is the God of gods and the LORD OF LORDS (אדוני האדונים).' The Hebrew preserves the Deuteronomy ordering. Greek uses the same order in TR, but the phrase originates from the Hebrew Bible.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: two companion terms — 'chosen ones and believers.' Greek: three terms — 'called, chosen, and faithful.' Greek adds 'called.'
translation_notes: 'Chosen ones' for b'chirim — the OT election term (Isa 42:1 — 'my chosen one'; 65:9 — 'my chosen ones shall inherit it').
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 10:17 — 'For YHWH your God is the God of gods and the Lord of lords (אדוני האדנים), the great, the mighty, and the awesome God.'

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to me: The waters{H4325} which you saw{H7200} where the harlot{H2181} sits{H3427} are peoples{H5971} and companies and nations{H523}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חַבְרוּתוֹת (chavrut'ot — 'companies/associations/fellowships') — from the root חבר (chaver — 'companion/friend'). This is a distinctly rabbinic/later Hebrew term (cf. chavruta — 'study partnership' in the Talmud). Greek ὄχλοι ('crowds/mobs') is entirely different — unorganized masses vs. organized associations. A back-translator from Greek 'crowds' would use הֲמוֹנִים (hamonim — 'multitudes') or קהלות (qehalot — 'assemblies'), NEVER the rabbinic chavrut'ot.

Uses אוּמִים (ummim — 'nations') — the later Hebrew form of אומה (ummah). This is NOT the standard biblical גּוֹי (goy — 'nation') or לְאוֹם (le'om — 'people'). The choice of this later Hebrew form is natural for a Hebrew writer but would never be chosen by a back-translator.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: THREE terms — 'peoples, companies, nations.' Greek: FOUR terms — 'peoples, multitudes, nations, tongues' (λαοὶ καὶ ὄχλοι... ἔθνη καὶ γλῶσσαι). Hebrew omits 'tongues' (γλῶσσαι).
Hebrew: 'companies' (organized). Greek: 'multitudes' (unorganized). Different social concept.

verses.translation: And the ten{H6235} horns{H7161} which you saw{H7200} upon the beast{H2416}, they shall be enemies{H8130} of the harlot{H2181} and shall make{H6213} desolation{H8077} of her, and shall eat{H398} her flesh{H1320}, and with fire{H784} they shall burn{H8313} her.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שְׁמָמָה (shemamah, H8077 — 'desolation') — the powerful OT word from the Levitical curses (Lev 26:33 — 'your land shall be a desolation'), the prophetic judgments (Isa 1:7, Jer 4:7, 25:11), and Daniel's 'abomination of desolation' (Dan 9:27 — שקוץ שמם). Greek ἠρημωμένην ('desolated') is a standard participle. The Hebrew shemamah carries the covenantal curse weight — this is the Torah's threatened punishment for faithlessness.
greek_deviations: Greek adds γυμνήν ('naked') — 'they shall make her desolate AND naked.' The nakedness element is absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Desolation' for shemamah preserves the Levitical curse and Danielic connections.
The burning of the harlot's flesh echoes the penalty for a priest's daughter who commits fornication (Lev 21:9 — 'she shall be burned with fire').
textual_notes: Leviticus 21:9 — 'And the daughter of any priest, if she profanes herself by playing the harlot (לזנות), she shall be burned with fire (באש תשרף).' The harlot receives the priestly-daughter penalty.

verses.translation: For YHWH{H3068} placed{H5414} in their hearts{H3820} to do{H6213} his will{H7522}: to give{H5414} her riches to the beast{H2416}, until the word{H1697} of YHWH{H3068} is fulfilled{H3615}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יַהְוֶה (YHWH, H3068) — the covenant name, TWICE. Greek has ὁ Θεός ('God') — the generic title. A back-translator from Greek Θεός would write אֱלֹהִים (Elohim — 'God'), not the specific Tetragrammaton. The Hebrew author naturally uses YHWH in a context about sovereign control over history.

Uses רְצוֹנוֹ (retsono — 'his will/desire/pleasure', H7522) — the specific OT word for divine will and favor (Ps 5:12, 30:5, 40:8, 51:18, 103:21, 143:10 — 'teach me to do your ratson'). Greek γνώμην αὐτοῦ ('his purpose/decision') is cognitive/intellectual. Hebrew ratson is volitional/relational — it's about YHWH's desire and pleasure, not merely his decree.

CRITICAL: Hebrew says עָשִׁרוּתֶיהָ (ashiruteha — 'HER riches') — they give the harlot's wealth to the beast. Greek says τὴν βασιλείαν αὐτῶν ('THEIR kingdom') — they give their own kingdom to the beast. FUNDAMENTALLY different: Hebrew — they transfer the harlot's wealth; Greek — they transfer their own sovereignty. A translation from one to the other cannot produce this divergence.
Uses דִּיבּוּרַת (dibburat — 'word of') — a later Hebrew form of דבר, natural in post-biblical Hebrew composition.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'YHWH' (covenant name, twice). Greek: 'God' (Θεός, generic title, twice). Major theological difference.
Hebrew: 'her riches' (עשירותיה). Greek: 'their kingdom' (τὴν βασιλείαν αὐτῶν). Different object and different possessor.
Hebrew: 'his will' (ratson — desire). Greek: 'his purpose' (γνώμη — decision).
translation_notes: 'Will' for ratson — this is about YHWH's sovereign pleasure, not merely an intellectual decree.
עָשִׁרוּתֶיהָ (ashiruteha — 'her riches') — later Hebrew form from עשר (osher — 'wealth'). No standard Strong's number.

verses.translation: And the woman{H802} which you saw{H7200} is the great{H1419} city{H5892} which reigns{H4427} over all{H3605} the kings{H4428} of the earth{H776}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַמֹּלֵךְ (hamolekh — 'which reigns', active participle from malakh H4427). Greek: ἡ ἔχουσα βασιλείαν ('the one HAVING a kingdom'). The Hebrew describes ACTIVE REIGNING — she is the one who reigns. The Greek describes POSSESSING a kingdom — she holds sovereignty as a possession. A back-translator from Greek would write שיש לה מלכות ('who has a kingdom'), not use the active reigning participle.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'reigns over' (active verb). Greek: 'has a kingdom over' (possession). Different mode of authority.

chapter_notes.summary: Revelation 17 in Hebrew contains at least 12 clear one-way translation markers. The most striking are: (1) כמראה שושנים ('like the appearance of roses') for the beast's color — a Hebrew botanical simile where Greek has a simple color word; (2) the היה ולא הוה wordplay using the root of YHWH's name to describe the beast's non-existence; (3) Sheol (שאול) vs. Greek 'destruction' (ἀπώλεια) for the beast's destination — consistently in v8 and v11; (4) סוד (sod — 'divine council secret') vs. Greek μυστήριον; (5) the three-part wisdom formula שכל וחכמה ותבונה; (6) YHWH (twice) vs. Greek Θεός; (7) 'her riches' vs. Greek 'their kingdom' — an irreconcilable divergence; (8) the anti-priestly forehead inscription echoing Exodus 28:38; (9) טומאות (Levitical impurity) vs. Greek βδελύγματα (abominations); and (10) אנשי האדמה ('men of the ground' — Genesis creation language) vs. Greek 'dwellers of the earth.' The chapter also shows consistent use of OT vocabulary: mishpat, qe'arot, midbar, chirufim, machashavah, shemamah, koach/gevurah — all deeply rooted in the Hebrew Bible.
